item.title: The Ground Under Naples Has Risen Four and a Half Feet: Inside Campi Flegrei's 40-Year Wake-Up Call
item.body:
On the last day of July, the ground west of Naples moved hard enough to close a working port.

The magnitude 4.7 earthquake that struck the Campi Flegrei caldera on July 31 was, by the reckoning of Italy's national geophysics institute, the strongest tremor the area has produced in roughly four decades. Twenty-six people were reported injured. Around 130 households were emptied while engineers checked walls and stairwells. The port of Pozzuoli — the ferry link to Ischia and Procida, and a piece of ordinary economic infrastructure for tens of thousands of people — was closed for inspection.

Those are the numbers that traveled. But they are not the story. The story is slower, quieter, and considerably stranger: the floor of the caldera has been rising, more or less continuously, for two decades. Since 2005, the ground at the center of the uplift has swelled by more than 140 centimeters — about four and a half feet.

That is not a metaphor. The coastline near Pozzuoli is physically higher than it was when the first iPhone shipped.

## What bradyseism actually is

The phenomenon has a name that predates modern volcanology: *bradyseism*, from the Greek for "slow movement." It describes the gradual rise and fall of the ground surface inside a volcanic caldera, driven not by lava but by pressure — hot fluids, gases, and possibly magma at depth pushing the rock above them upward like a slow hydraulic jack, then letting it settle again.

Campi Flegrei is the textbook case. The Romans built a market at Pozzuoli, the Macellum, whose surviving columns carry a band of holes bored by marine mollusks several meters above the modern floor. Those holes are a tide gauge running two thousand years long. The ground sank below sea level, sat there for centuries, and rose again. Naples has been living on a piston this whole time.

The caldera itself is about 12 to 15 kilometers across, and most of it is not a mountain. It is a shallow bowl of neighborhoods, ports, thermal baths, and highways, partly submerged under the Gulf of Pozzuoli, partly overlapping the western districts of Naples proper. Roughly half a million people live inside it. That density — European, coastal, historic, and built long before anyone modeled seismic loads — is the variable that turns a geophysics problem into a civil-protection problem.

## Why a 4.7 hurts more here

A magnitude 4.7 is not a large earthquake by global standards. In many parts of the world it would rattle dishes and make the local news for one cycle.

Campi Flegrei is different for two reasons.

**The quakes are extremely shallow.** Most caldera seismicity here originates within a few kilometers of the surface, some of it much shallower than that. Energy that would dissipate through the crust on its way up from a 30-kilometer hypocenter instead arrives almost immediately, concentrated under a small area. The shaking is sharp, loud, and disproportionate to the magnitude number.

**The buildings have been strained for years, not seconds.** This is the point most easily lost. Uplift does not merely precede earthquakes; it deforms structures directly. A masonry building whose foundation has tilted and stretched a few centimeters over a decade is not the same building it was — it has accumulated cracks, lost stiffness, and shed some of its margin. When the sharp shock finally arrives, it lands on a structure already partway through its budget. That is why local damage reports tend to describe cornices, stairwells, and older masonry rather than dramatic collapses, and it is why Italy's building-survey program in the area has focused on cumulative vulnerability rather than any single event.

## Rising ground is not a countdown

Here is the part that deserves care, because it is where public understanding usually goes wrong.

Uplift is not a schedule. Campi Flegrei has been at the "yellow" attention level in Italy's four-tier volcanic alert system since 2012 — a designation that means monitoring has been intensified and parameters are being tracked closely, not that an eruption has been forecast. The system has three levels above yellow, and moving between them requires specific, agreed-upon changes in the data.

Researchers broadly work with two overlapping explanations for the current unrest, and the honest answer is that they are difficult to separate from the surface:

- **A hydrothermal interpretation.** Superheated water and gas — much of it originating from magma sitting several kilometers down — migrate into shallow rock, pressurize it, and lift it. This can produce years of uplift, gas emission, and shallow seismicity without magma itself rising to shallow depth.
- **A magmatic interpretation.** A body of magma at depth is intruding or degassing more actively, driving the same signals from below.

Both produce uplift. Both produce earthquakes. The discriminating evidence tends to come from gas chemistry, deformation patterns, and how the crust responds to repeated stress — and recent work has emphasized a third factor that complicates the picture: after decades of being stretched and shaken, the shallow crust here may simply be weaker than it was, meaning it fractures at lower stress than it used to. Under that reading, more frequent earthquakes are partly a sign of a fatigued lid, not necessarily a stronger push from beneath.

That is a genuinely important nuance, and it cuts both ways. It offers a less alarming explanation for rising quake counts. It also means the system's behavior is changing in ways that make historical analogies less reliable.

## The 1982–84 precedent

The last major bradyseismic crisis ran from 1982 to 1984 and lifted the ground at Pozzuoli by roughly 1.8 meters. Tens of thousands of residents were relocated; the old town core of Rione Terra was evacuated and stayed largely empty for years afterward. Then the ground stopped, settled somewhat, and the crisis ended without an eruption.

That is the most useful precedent available, and it points in a reassuring direction — sustained, meters-scale uplift ended quietly. But the current episode has now run far longer than that one, at a slower rate, and it is arriving in a place with two more generations of construction on top of it.

## What is being watched, and what would change the assessment

If you want to follow this the way monitoring agencies do, the meaningful indicators are not the magnitude headlines. They are:

- **Uplift rate**, measured in millimeters per month by GPS stations and satellite radar. Acceleration matters far more than the accumulated total.
- **Earthquake depth.** Persistent shallow activity fits the hydrothermal picture. A sustained migration of seismicity toward the surface, or new activity at intermediate depths, would be a different signal.
- **Gas chemistry** at the Solfatara and Pisciarelli fumarole fields — particularly the ratios of carbon dioxide to water vapor and helium isotopes, which help distinguish a magmatic contribution from a purely hydrothermal one.
- **Ground temperature and emission flux**, which track how much heat the system is moving.

None of those has a single threshold that flips a switch. Alert-level changes are made on a package of evidence by a national commission, not on any one reading.

## The practical layer

For residents and visitors, the operative guidance is unglamorous and comes from Italy's Civil Protection Department and municipal authorities, not from any article:

- Know whether your address falls in the designated hazard zones, and know the assigned assembly points and evacuation route — the local comune publishes them.
- Keep the standard earthquake habits: secure heavy furniture, know which interior wall or doorway you would move to, keep documents and medications somewhere you can grab them.
- Treat official channels as the source of truth during an event. Aftershock sequences in this caldera routinely produce a wave of speculation that outruns the data by hours.
- If a building has been posted as unusable after inspection, that assessment reflects strain that is not always visible from the street.

## The wider point

Campi Flegrei is a stress test for something more general than volcanology. It is what happens when a slow-moving natural hazard sits under a place people cannot simply leave — where the housing is old, the economy is local, the deadline is unknown, and the honest scientific answer is "we are monitoring it, and it may go on like this for years."

The port reopens. The households return or they don't. The instruments keep logging millimeters. Four and a half feet accumulated in twenty-one years is not a headline on any single day, which is precisely why it took a magnitude 4.7 to make anyone outside Naples look at it.

---

*This article summarizes publicly reported information and the current published scientific understanding of the Campi Flegrei caldera. Figures on damage, injuries, and displacement reflect initial official reports and are commonly revised. It is general information, not emergency guidance — for situation-specific instructions, follow Italy's Civil Protection Department and local municipal authorities.*
